newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel police chief warns of attacks over settlement.
newsitem.headline: Israel police chief warns of attacks over settlement.

text.p: Israel's police chief said on Wednesday the construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem had harmed security cooperation with the PLO and raised the likelihood of guerrilla attacks.

His assessment came as Israeli bulldozers, for a second day, ripped into the pine-covered hill called Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa in Hebrew, angering Palestinians and drawing international condemnation.

"The new situation between the (Palestinian) Authority and Israel is worse than when we had cooperation and dialogue which...guaranteed there would be no guerrilla attacks," police chief Assaf Hefetz told reporters.
"I think this situation has changed and for this reason security officials feel that attacks could take place," he said.
Palestinian officials said they were doing all they could to prevent violence but warned an angry outburst was inevitable.
"We are (headed) for an explosion," said Faisal al-Husseini, the PLO's top official in Jerusalem.
"When it will start, what will be the spark, I don't know. But I can be sure...that and explosion is coming if the situation will not be changed," Husseini told reporters.
In the West Bank village of Beit Umar, Israeli soldiers fired teargas to disperse stone-throwers during a brief incident that ended without injuries, witnesses said.
Hundreds of Palestinians marched in the self-ruled towns of Bethlehem and Ramallah in protest at the project. Palestinian police kept them away from Israeli roadblocks.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said PLO authorities had "severed contacts" with Israel and were withholding cooperation on security matters.

An army spokesman said Israeli and Palestinian troops had stopped patrolling together in the West Bank for now. The two sides last halted joint patrols in September after 61 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in violence sparked by Israeli moves in East Jerusalem.

Israeli and PLO security officials had been cooperating since a landmark 1993 peace deal to thwart Islamic guerrillas opposed to their accord. Hamas and Islamic Jihad militants have killed scores of Israelis in suicide bombings.
In Egypt, President Hosni Mubarak said Israel was leading the region into a new era of violence. Syria accused Netanyahu of bringing the region to the brink of war.
"Mr Netanyahu's policy has killed the peace process. We're trying to defend this peace process (but) I don't think it's any more there," Husseini said.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected criticism of Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on land between Jerusalem and Bethlehem it captured in the 1967 Middle East war, saying it was part of the Israeli capital.
"I can't imagine any peace process under which we can't build in our capital," he told Israel Radio on Wednesday. "I don't agree to any peace that prevents us from building in Jerusalem."
Palestinians view East Jerusalem as their future capital.
Israel's Supreme Court on Wednesday heard two legal challenges against the plan to build 6,500 Jewish homes on the hill but refused to issue orders to temporarily suspend work.
A court spokesman said a third petition would be heard at a later date.
The United States, Israel's closest ally, said on Tuesday peace efforts could be crushed by the Israeli project. Officials in Washington urged Israel and the Palestinians to resume talks.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) called for an immediate meeting of the United Nations Security Council to demand a halt to the settlement.
